why: The shapes a real `python` on PATH can present, and what each installer half
must make of them. Both halves ask the same question -- print MAJOR MINOR --
so the only thing that varies is what the interpreter says back, and on which
stream. That is what these cases are.
and install.sh::_system_python_version. Cases belong here, never inline in the
test module: an inline case is a case only one half is held to, which is the
hole this closes -- the same one extras-contract.json closes for #648/#653.

cases.why: The ordinary machine: the answer on stdout, silence elsewhere, exit 0.

stderr: Python was not found; run without arguments to install from the Microsoft Store, or disable this shortcut from Settings > Manage App Execution Aliases.
cases.why: A fresh Windows box with no Python still has a 0-byte Store App Execution Alias on PATH. Declining sends the caller to a uv-managed Python; throwing here is what aborted the install in the Python stage.
A perfectly usable Python that warns on stderr on the way past -- a conda banner, a DLL or deprecation notice. It answered; the noise is not the answer.
An interpreter that greets on stdout puts a non-numeric line ahead of the answer. The version is the LAST line; reading the first one is an [int] cast (or a shell arithmetic test) on a word.
'Last line' has to mean last NON-EMPTY line, or a trailing blank becomes the version.
The probe reports, it does not judge. Whether 3.13 is acceptable is the caller's min/max policy, and keeping that out of here is what lets the caller warn precisely instead of just falling back.
A nonzero exit means the interpreter did not answer the question, whatever it happened to print.
Exit 0 is not enough on its own: the strict match is what actually vouches for the answer.
Silent success is not a version. It is also what a stale exit code looks like when the command never ran at all.
Half an answer is not an answer; taking it would leave MINOR unset and compare it as an empty string.
Not the format either half asked for. Guards against a probe loose enough to accept `python --version` output, where the leading word would be 'Python'.
